title: I am Time
hookLine: the line Oppenheimer remembered, and what the Sanskrit word actually says
carry: time is god's; i'm only the instrument
last: VISHVARUPA — THE WHOLE UNIVERSE IN ONE GOD.

cards: The New Mexico desert, before dawn. A bomb is tested, and a blinding light fills the sky. Years later, in a 1965 television documentary, J.
Robert Oppenheimer, who led the scientists who built it, remembered what went through his mind. He had studied Sanskrit and read the Gita in the original.
He recalled a line, in his own words: now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds. So what does the Sanskrit actually say?

teach.b: Verse thirty-two begins: kalo 'smi. I am kala. Kala means time.
It can also carry the sense of death, the way time eventually brings everything to an end, which is how Oppenheimer rendered it.
The verse goes on: I am time, grown mighty, destroyer of worlds, here to bring the worlds to their end.

teach.h: EVEN WITHOUT YOU, NONE WILL SURVIVE.
teach.b: Then the line that hits Arjuna hardest: even without you, none of these warriors lined up in the opposing ranks will survive.
Back in chapter one, Arjuna broke down at the thought of killing his teachers and his great-uncle. Krishna's answer is that time has already claimed them. Verse thirty-three: so stand up, win glory.
They've already been struck down by me.
You be only the instrument. Nimitta-matram: merely the occasion, the tool.

teach.h: A REAL WAR, OR THE WAR WITHIN.
teach.b: Verse thirty-four names them: Drona, Bhishma, Karna, and the rest, already slain. Don't be distressed. Fight.

This is one of the hardest passages in the Gita, and readers have taken it in very different ways. Some read it as it stands: a warrior's duty in a just war, and the truth that no one controls who lives and who dies.
Mahatma Gandhi read the whole battlefield as an allegory of the war inside each person, and took the Gita as a teaching of nonviolence.
Either way, it lands on a core Hindu teaching: do your dharma, your rightful part, as God's instrument, and don't claim to be the one who controls how it ends.
The ending belongs to time, and time, Krishna says, is him.

how: Hindus read Gita 11.32–34 in different ways: some as a warrior's duty and the power of time over every life, others, following Gandhi, as an allegory of the inner battle; the image of Kala, time, also appears in the worship of Shiva and Kali.

games.why: nimitta-matram bhava: be only the instrument. time has already struck them down.

practice: Listen for time: a clock ticking, your heartbeat, the breath coming and going, each one arriving and leaving, none of them staying. Then think of one thing you're trying to control the ending of.
If you pray, offer it the way many Hindus do after an action, with one word: Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna. If not, just set the ending down. Your part is the next breath.

wordCard.voice: Kala. Time, which brings everything to its end. Gita eleven, thirty-two: grown mighty, destroyer of worlds. Oppenheimer rendered it as death.

orig.note: Sanskrit: kalo 'smi, 'I am time' (11.32); kala, time, also the time that ends all things.

carryVoice: Your line: time is God's; I'm only the instrument. It's Krishna's answer to who are you. That's day one hundred ninety-eight.
